This is Danza de los Voladores. Pre-Hispanic.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The ritual is believed to have originated with the Nahua, Huastec, and Otomi peoples in central Mexico.
It is associated with pre-Hispanic fertility cults and was used to appease gods during severe droughts.
Evidence of the ritual exists in ceramics from the pre-Classic period in Nayarit.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The ritual is performed to request rain, ensure fertility, and honor solar deities.
It is often linked to the spring equinox and the patron saint feast days of local communities.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The ceremony involves climbing a 30-meter pole.
The caporal stands on a small platform at the top, playing a flute and drum.
Four other participants sit on a square frame, wind ropes around the pole, and then fall backward to descend while spinning in a circle.
Watch for The Descent.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is performed by the caporal using a flute and a drum.
The music is described as representing the sound of birds singing and is used to acknowledge the four cardinal directions.
Listen for the Flute, Drum.
The music consists of a flute and drum played by the caporal at the top of the pole, representing the sound of birds singing.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear red pants, white shirts, and an embroidered cloth across the chest.
The cap is decorated with flowers, mirrors, and multicolored ribbons.
The setting is a 30-meter pole, traditionally made from a tree trunk, though modern poles are often metal.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Jesús Arroyo Cerón is noted as a significant trainer of voladores, including female participants, who died during a performance in 2006.

Variations include the number of dancers (sometimes six), the use of a five-sided frame, and the inclusion of women in specific Puebla and Veracruz communities, which remains a subject of debate among elders.
The ritual is a Mesoamerican tradition that spread from central Mexico to Nicaragua, surviving primarily among the Totonac and Nahua peoples.
